parsed.summary: The Lean statement says that for every complex s with Re s > 7/8, Mathlib's `riemannZeta s ≠ 0`. This is exactly the ζ-case of the paper's main theorem, i.e. the quasi-Riemann hypothesis with σ₀ = 7/8. The most important caveat is coverage: the Hecke L-functions over ℚ(√-3) and general Dirichlet L-functions in Theorem 1 are not formalized. A minor point is that the Lean statement also asserts nonvanishing at the pole s = 1, where it refers to Mathlib's convention value. That value is known to be nonzero (`riemannZeta_one_ne_zero`), so the extra claim is true and costless.

glossary.plain: Mathlib's Riemann zeta function on ℂ: the meromorphic continuation of Σ n^{-s}, totalized at s = 1 by the value (γ − log 4π)/2.
glossary.note: Agrees with ζ away from s = 1. At s = 1 it takes a finite, nonzero convention value.

lean_claims.plain: For all s ∈ ℂ with 7/8 < Re s, riemannZeta s ≠ 0. This includes s = 1, where the claim is about the convention value.

paper_claims.plain: Every finite-order Hecke L-function over F = ℚ(√-3) has no zero in Re s > 7/8. The same holds for every Dirichlet L-function, including ζ(s). A pole at s = 1 for a principal character is allowed.
ζ(s) ≠ 0 for Re s > 7/8. Equivalently, the supremum of the real parts of the nontrivial zeros of ζ is at most 7/8.

coverage.why: Same half-plane and same nonvanishing claim. The additional assertion at s = 1 is the true Mathlib fact `riemannZeta_one_ne_zero`.
No Hecke L-function statement appears in the Lean file.
Only the trivial character (ζ) is covered. No statement about DirichletCharacter.LFunction is made.

flags.explanation: The paper's main theorem is uniform over all Dirichlet L-functions and all finite-order Hecke L-functions over ℚ(√-3). The Lean statement covers only ζ. The quasi-RH corollary is fully captured, but the uniform statement is not.
flags.probe_idea: Formalize: ∀ {q} (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ q) (s : ℂ), 7/8 < s.re → (χ ≠ 1 ∨ s ≠ 1) → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s ≠ 0

flags.paper_ref: Theorem 1 ('A pole at s = 1 ... is allowed')
flags.explanation: The hypotheses do not exclude the pole s = 1, so the statement also asserts riemannZeta 1 ≠ 0, a convention value the paper says nothing about. In practice this is harmless: Mathlib already proves `riemannZeta_one_ne_zero` (the value is (γ − log 4π)/2 < 0). The extra claim is true and adds no substantive content.

lint_verdicts.why: (7 / 8 : ℝ) is real division and equals 0.875; there is no truncation.
The region contains the pole s = 1, but Mathlib's convention value there is provably nonzero (`riemannZeta_one_ne_zero`).
Same as line 5: the claim at s = 1 is the known true fact riemannZeta 1 ≠ 0.
